identification: Single-sided vitreous enamel advertising strip sign, white sans-serif letters on cobalt blue: 'LEADING NEWSPAPER. / THE DAILY TELEGRAPH. / TASMANIA.' with 'MADE IN ENGLAND' small at lower right. 15 x 53 cm (catalogue). The Daily Telegraph was the Launceston daily paper (1883 to 1928, when it merged into The Examiner), so the sign predates 1928, probably 1900s to 1920s. Condition: top right corner has a large chunk missing or torn away with rust along the broken edge (the plate outline steps down there, so this is metal loss, not just chipping); small chips and rust at the fixing holes along top and bottom edges and at the corners; face enamel otherwise bright with good gloss and little fading. Back (photo 4) is rusted with green/grey counter-enamel and white enamel drips, consistent with genuine period enamel, not a modern reproduction (reproductions are usually printed tin or have clean backs).

viewing_check: Check the broken corner: is the metal torn off (loss) or bent back? Look along the bottom and back edges for an enameller's name (Wildman, Patent Enamel, Chromo, Falkirk, Bruton). Check the back is heavy steel with counter-enamel (genuine) rather than thin tin. Note chip count around the holes.
